blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
McNemar’s test (McNemar, 1947) tests paired binary data: the same subjects measured twice, two raters classifying the same subjects, or matched case-control pairs. Arrange the pairs in a 2 × 2 table of pairs. Let b and c be the two kinds of discordant pairs (the members of the pair differ). Then

X²_McNemar = (b − c)² ÷ (b + c), on 1 df.

For a matched case-control study the matched-pair odds ratio is OR = b/c, with SE(ln OR) = √(1/b + 1/c).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The chi-square test of independence assumes independent observations. Paired data are not independent: a household measured before and after an education drive is the same household. Pairs in which both members agree (concordant pairs) say nothing about which way things shifted. Only the discordant pairs carry information, and under H₀ each of them is equally likely to go either way.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. Under H₀, each of the b + c discordant pairs is of type “b” with probability 0.5. So b ~ Binomial(b + c, 0.5): this is the sign test (§10.1.1) applied to the discordant pairs.
  2. For large b + c, b is approximately Normal with mean (b + c)/2 and SD √[(b + c)/4] (recall §5.7.2.2.4).
  3. z = [b − (b + c)/2] ÷ √[(b + c)/4] = (b − c) ÷ √(b + c), so z² = (b − c)² ÷ (b + c).
  4. In a matched case-control study, the concordant pairs match cases and controls on exposure and so cannot contribute to a contrast within the pair. Among discordant pairs, the odds that the case (rather than the control) is the exposed one is b/c, which is the matched OR. The same estimate comes out of conditional logistic regression (§13.2.9, a regression model that compares each case only with its own matched controls).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Before and after. To test whether CBHI membership changes after a community education drive in the same 100 households, a χ² test of independence would wrongly treat “before” and “after” as two independent samples. McNemar’s test compares the households that joined with those that dropped out.

Matched case-control. Eighty children with diarrhoea (cases) were each matched to a control child of the same age from the same village. Exposure: not exclusively breastfed in infancy.

Control exposed Control not exposed
Case exposed 16 (concordant) b = 24
Case not exposed c = 10 30 (concordant)

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Discordant pairs: b = 24, c = 10; b + c = 34. The 46 concordant pairs drop out.
  2. X² = (24 − 10)² ÷ 34 = 196 ÷ 34 = 5.76, 1 df, p = 0.016.
  3. With a continuity correction: (|24 − 10| − 1)² ÷ 34 = 169 ÷ 34 = 4.97, p = 0.026. The exact binomial version (the sign test of §10.1.1 on the 34 discordant pairs) gives p = 0.024.
  4. Matched OR = 24/10 = 2.4. SE(ln OR) = √(1/24 + 1/10) = 0.376. CI: exp(0.875 ± 1.96 × 0.376) = 1.15 to 5.02.
  5. Ignoring the matching: pooled into an ordinary 2 × 2 table, 40 of 80 cases and 26 of 80 controls were exposed, and ad/bc = (40 × 54)/(40 × 26) = 2.08. In this dataset the unmatched analysis gives a different, smaller OR. Matched data must be analysed as matched.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
m  <- read.csv("data/matched_casecontrol.csv")
cs <- m[m$case == 1, ]; ct <- m[m$case == 0, ]
pp <- merge(cs, ct, by = "pair_id", suffixes = c(".case", ".ctrl"))
pt <- table(case = factor(pp$not_ebf.case, levels = 1:0),
            control = factor(pp$not_ebf.ctrl, levels = 1:0))
pt
mcnemar.test(pt, correct = FALSE)
b <- pt[1, 2]; c <- pt[2, 1]
# matched OR and its 95% CI
exp(log(b / c) + c(0, -1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(1/b + 1/c))
    control
case  1  0
   1 16 24
   0 10 30

    McNemar's Chi-squared test

data:  pt
McNemar's chi-squared = 5.7647, df = 1, p-value = 0.01635

[1] 2.400000 1.147690 5.018775

merge puts each case beside its own control, and the table of pairs is the one above. McNemar’s X² is step 2, and the last line is the matched OR with its CI from step 4. (mcnemar.test(pt) without correct = FALSE gives the corrected 4.97.)

points.html: Paired binary data → McNemar; independent groups → χ² or Fisher. It is the categorical counterpart of the paired t-test.
Only discordant pairs enter the test and the matched OR. When b + c is small, use the exact binomial version (step 3), for the same reason as in §10.1.1.
For paired data with more than two categories, Bowker’s test of symmetry extends the same discordant-pairs logic.
Chance-corrected agreement between two raters on the same subjects is a different question, answered by kappa (§16.3.3.1); McNemar tests only whether one rater says “yes” more often than the other.

questions.prompt: A 2 × 2 table has three expected counts below 5. Which test should you use, and why is Yates’ correction not the answer?
questions.answer: Fisher’s exact test. It computes the p-value exactly from the hypergeometric distribution, with the margins fixed, so it does not rely on the χ² approximation. Yates’ correction only adjusts the approximation for the discreteness of counts; it does not repair an approximation that fails because expected counts are too small (the §10.7 pilot shows uncorrected p = 0.036, Yates p = 0.126, exact p = 0.091).

questions.prompt: In a before–after survey of 150 households, 20 joined CBHI and 8 left; the rest did not change. Compute McNemar’s X² and state your conclusion at the 5% level.
questions.answer: Discordant pairs: b = 20 (joined), c = 8 (left). X² = (20 − 8)² ÷ (20 + 8) = 144 ÷ 28 = 5.14, 1 df, p = 0.023. Membership rose significantly after the drive: more households joined than left. (The 122 unchanged households do not enter the test. The exact binomial version, the sign test on the 28 discordant pairs, gives p = 0.036, the same conclusion.)

questions.prompt: In a matched case-control study, b = 30 and c = 12. Compute the matched OR and its 95% CI.
